description:
Signal to Noise, a crew of CS Data Science students who have some experience in computer vision and ML, are joining the SARs to dance. We will be mapping the flooding in the Philippines using the NISAR radar that can penetrate clouds, and create an interactive change-detection map, along with ML water segmentation.

We are seeking web developers (maps/frontend), data analysts and a designer or storyteller for our pitch. The following are desirable: an interest in Earth Science.
summary:
We built an interactive Streamlit web app that uses NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band radar data to track how the August 2026 storms (Luis, Maymay and the southwest monsoon) flooded farmland around the Candaba Swamp in Pampanga, Central Luzon, the area hit hardest by rice losses in the province.

We use a pipeline that removes radar speckle, maps open storm flood outside the area's typical water, flags experimental “hidden flood” under standing crops and counts the number of consecutive 12-day passes for which each field remained under water from nine NISAR GCOV passes (June 23 to October 9, 2026). When combined with ESA WorldCover cropland and municipal boundaries, the app is able to display cropland at high risk of crop loss, and rank municipalities by impact.

This is the solution for the Dancing with the SARs challenge: It is transforming the complex radar data into clear maps and into a before/after timeline and ranking that can be understood by anyone. It's important because typhoon clouds obscure optical satellites during the time of flood occurrence. Radar can peer through them and provide farmers, local governments, the Department of Agriculture and crop insurers with evidence to speed up targeting of aid and recovery.
details:
What it is and how it works.

Our Streamlit web app shows the flooding of farmland around the Candaba Swamp, Pampanga during the August 2026 storms. Nine of the NASA-ISRO NISAR L2 GCOV radar passes were used, from June 23 to October 9, 2026, track 140 ascending, frame 9, dual-pol HH/HV, which were downloaded via ASF with a NASA Earthdata Login. The images derived from each scene are cropped to the area of the study, speckled cleaned using a Lee filter, and reprojected to a common grid to be pixel for pixel date synchronized.

The water detection is done at HH backscatter level under –14 dB. Normal water is from the July 5 and 17 pre-storm scenes, plus JRC Global Surface Water, while storm flood is water after that. The HH double bounce signal of the L-band is an experimental “hidden flood” layer that flags water under standing crops with the HH signal rising more than 3 dB above the HV signal near open flood. The number of consecutive 12-day passes a pixel remained flooded is counted and cropland that was flooded for two or more passes is classified as being at high risk for crop loss. The geoBoundaries were used to summarize the results per municipality.

Benefits and intended impact

Optical satellites are unable to capture typhoon clouds just when floods occur. They can be seen through, day and night, by radar. The app depicts flood extents, duration of exposure to flooding, and municipalities with the highest proportion of cropland at risk. This can facilitate the Department of Agriculture, local governments and crop insurers to prioritize aid, recovery and claims more quickly.

Creativity

We didn't just ask 'where's the water' and now ask ‘how long is it going to last and what does it mean for farms’. We took advantage of the fact that L-band is sensitive to water under vegetation and distinguished the swamp's seasonal water from the flooding of a storm.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty. The pass of the 23rd June is not included in the baseline because it is a false alarm test, and provides our margin of error.

Sensitivity. All results were rerun at −15 dB to demonstrate the threshold sensitivity of the results.

Use clear labels such as ‘high risk of crop loss' instead of ‘rice lost', since there are many swamp fields which contain fishponds in the wet season.

Limits of the data: PROVISIONAL NISAR data, and the Jul 27 – Aug 10 data gap.

Tools

Python (NumPy, SciPy, rasterio, h5py, pyproj, GeoPandas, scikit-image, pandas, asf_search), Google Colab, Google Drive, Streamlit and GitHub. No special hardware was employed.
